abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces the Socio-Technical Alignment Framework (STAF), a novel theoretical perspective that reconceptualizes the relationship between social dynamics and interactive systems in computer-supported cooperative work. Traditional HCI theories have predominantly treated social and technical elements as separable components, yet emerging challenges in complex collaborative environments demand more integrated approaches. STAF proposes that social meaning-making and interface affordances co-constitute user experience through iterative alignment processes, challenging the dominant cognitive processing paradigm in human-computer interaction. Through a meta-analysis of 87 empirical studies examining distributed teams' interaction patterns, we identify four fundamental alignment mechanisms: reciprocal adaptation, artifact mediation, boundary negotiation, and emergent coordination. Our theoretical contributions are threefold: First, we establish a unified conceptual vocabulary for describing social-technical interdependence in interactive systems. Second, we introduce the Alignment Dynamics Model, which explains how users progressively construct shared understanding through interface engagement. Third, we derive design principles that translate theoretical constructs into actionable guidelines for social computing platforms. This paradigmatic shift from individual cognition to distributed alignment offers new directions for interaction design research and provides researchers with evaluative instruments for assessing social aspects of collaborative technologies.

Despite extensive research on usability evaluation methods, existing approaches inadequately capture the temporal dynamics of user experience in mobile interaction contexts. This paper extends the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) by incorporating longitudinal usability dimensions and proposing the Dynamic TAM (D-TAM), which accounts for how perceived usefulness and ease of use evolve through sustained device engagement. Building upon human factors research in mobile computing, we conducted a longitudinal study with 156 participants across 12 weeks, collecting data through experience sampling, structured interviews, and behavioral telemetry from smartphone applications. Our analysis reveals three distinct usability trajectory patterns: progressive adaptation, initial decline followed by recovery, and continuous degradation, each with distinguishable predictors. The D-TAM demonstrates superior predictive validity (R² = 0.67) compared to the original TAM (R² = 0.48) for forecasting continued mobile application usage. We contribute an improved theoretical model that integrates usability engineering principles with acceptance theories, operationalize temporal usability constructs through validated measurement scales, and provide evaluation methods for practitioners to predict user engagement trajectories. These findings offer refined guidance for designing mobile interfaces that sustain positive user experience across extended interaction periods.

This paper presents HaptoMirror, a paradigmatic input device that enables bi-directional haptic communication through a reflective surface integrating vibrotactile actuators and pressure-sensitive force sensors. Unlike conventional haptic feedback systems that transmit unidirectional sensations, HaptoMirror establishes a novel interaction modality where users simultaneously send and receive tactile information, fundamentally reconceiving how physical contact mediates remote communication. Our system implements a spatial haptic rendering engine that translates body contact patterns into coordinated vibrotactile stimuli with 3ms latency and 16 distinct intensity levels. We developed three interaction techniques optimized for the bi-directional haptic channel: contact gestures, pressure signatures, and rhythmic patterns, each evaluated through controlled experiments. A user study with 48 participants comparing HaptoMirror against audio-only communication revealed significant improvements in interpersonal rapport (p < 0.001), emotional attunement (p < 0.01), and presence perception (p < 0.001). The paradigm innovation lies in our Spatial Contact Model, which conceptualizes haptic interaction as shared tactile space rather than isolated feedback events. This work opens new research directions for immersion technologies and social computing applications requiring intimate remote interaction, demonstrating that bi-directional haptics can fundamentally transform mediated communication experiences.

Existing screen reader technologies inadequately support visually impaired users in comprehending complex data visualizations, creating significant accessibility barriers in information-rich interactive systems. This paper presents DataSonify Pro, an improved accessible data exploration system that advances non-visual data representation through adaptive sonification and tactile-graphic synchronization. Our system improves upon prior approaches by introducing three key innovations: hierarchical audio rendering that conveys multi-dimensional data relationships, real-time tactile feedback synchronized with audio streams, and a configurable multi-modal pipeline allowing users to personalize sensory representations. The architecture integrates a novel Data Interpretation Layer that transforms visualization semantics into perceptually coherent audio-tactile mappings while preserving statistical relationships. We conducted a comparative evaluation with 32 participants with visual impairments, comparing DataSonify Pro against standard screen readers and commercial accessible visualization tools. Results demonstrate substantial improvements in task completion time (42% reduction), information comprehension accuracy (38% improvement), and user satisfaction (71% increase). The system successfully supports accessibility requirements across diverse visualization types including charts, graphs, and spatial data representations. Our contribution includes both the functional system implementation and validated design patterns for accessible interactive data visualization that can inform future developments in universal design for information interfaces.
